doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Volunteering for submarine service
summary: He chose submarines from midshipman school and was oddly selected despite failing the engineering questions.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: What made you pursue the submarine school?

Well I don’t know. I was in the midshipman’s school at Columbia. And there were I think 1,200 of us. And they put up lists, what did you want to do. And I got to thinking about the fact that most all the guys who were basically civilians like me got to do landing craft. And I thought that was a terrible way to end your life. And I wasn’t a flyer, but submarine service offered a lot of things. It offered first of all 50 percent increase in pay. It offered wonderful food, excellent food, and a pretty good life. And it was distinctive. You were one of five or six thousand of us in the war and that’s it. And we are a pretty distinctive breed really. So I volunteered for it. And they then sent a team around of three people: a commanding officer, an engineering officer and a mustang, that is a guy who came up from the ranks and who is rough and tough and so on. And they interviewed each of us. And I didn’t know the answers to any of the questions. I was an English literature major, and the engineering guy said, “What’s the difference between AC and DC current?” I said, “Dammed if I know.” And I was just honest about it. And I figured well that’s gone. Well as it turned out there were five of us that they picked. Four engineers and me, which obviously was a mistake. Somebody got the wrong number. It couldn’t have been me. So I went to submarine school. And the first thing they do, they spent two weeks with a nut house trying to figure out whether you can stand the pressure, and whether you get along with people well, and schizophrenia and all that stuff. And if you pass that you’re home free. You have to graduate from the school. They won’t let you flunk. I was the only one to pass out of the five of us. The four engineers went out to the amphibious fleet. So there I was. And I was in submarines and submarine school. I had a wonderful time.
I guess you don’t suffer from claustrophobia.
Oh no. Well looking back it was pretty tough but when you’re young and there’s a war on, a war that everybody wants to win, that was pretty nifty. I enjoyed every minute of it.
